pages.title: Introduction to API
pages.content:
Before we dive into building APIs…
Have you ever thought about this? 

**How does data actually come to your app?**
- You click buttons every day.
- You see data on screens all the time.
- But how does that data arrive there?

**Let’s find out by using a demo API first.**

---

**Open your browser and type this URL:**
```sss
https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1
```
Press `Enter`. \
**You will see something like this:**
```json
{
 "id": 1,
 "name": "Leanne Graham",
 "email": "leanne@example.com"
}
```
This **format** is called **JSON**.

**You just made an API call.** \
There was no login page and no buttons or screens — just data returned directly by a server. \
**This is exactly how an API works.**

---

**What just happened?**
- You typed a URL
- The browser sent a request
- Some server sent back data
- The data came in JSON format

**This data response is the result of an API call.**

pages.title: What Is an API (Application Programming Interface)
pages.content:
Imagine you go to a restaurant. 
- **You** are the customer (**User**/**Frontend**)
- **The chef(kitchen)** prepares the food (**backend**/**server**)
- **The waiter** takes your order to the chef and brings the food back to you (the **API**)

You never walk into the kitchen or talk to the chef directly. The waiter handles all communication between you and the kitchen.

---

In an application, an API works like the **waiter** in a restaurant.

Just like you don’t go into the kitchen or talk to the chef directly, an app or user never talks to the backend or database directly. **The API stands for Application Programming Interface that takes the request from the app, passes it to the backend (the chef), and then brings the response back**.

In simple words, **an API is a way for one application to communicate with another application**.

pages.title: How the Request - Response flow works
pages.content:
You’ve already seen how a restaurant works — you place an order, the waiter communicates with the kitchen, and the food comes back to you. \
Now let’s use that same example to understand how **requests and responses** work in applications.

---

**When you place an order in a restaurant:**

1. You place the order
2. The waiter takes it to the kitchen
3. The chef prepares the food
4. The waiter brings the food back to you


**The same idea applies to applications.**

1. The app sends a request
2. The API forwards the request to the backend
3. The backend processes it
4. The API sends back a response




---

**Key takeaway** \
Every time you see data on your screen, this request → response flow has already happened. \
The **API** is the **middle layer** that makes this communication possible.

This is the exact flow you will implement when you start building APIs using **Spring Boot** in the next section.

practiceProblems.description:
**Look at the given code in your IDE**. You can see that the `getUser()` method returns some data in the form of a Map. \
Don’t focus on `@GetMapping` or `@RestController` for now. \
**Let’s first understand what JSON is and how APIs use it**.

---

When you run this API and access the endpoint, the output looks like this:
```json
{
 "id": "1",
 "name": "Leanne Graham",
 "email": "leanne@example.com"
}
```

This is **JSON**, a standard format APIs use to **exchange data** between servers and clients (like web browsers, mobile apps, or other services).

---

**What is JSON?**
- **JSON** = JavaScript Object Notation
- A **lightweight, human-readable format** for data
- Structured with **key-value pairs**, like a Java Map
- Here, In JSON output :
 - `"id"`, `"name"`, `"email"` → keys
 - `"1"`, `"Leanne Graham"`, `"leanne@example.com"` → values
 - Values can also be numbers, arrays, or nested objects

---

**How APIs Use JSON**
1. **Sending Data (Response)**
- API sends JSON to clients (browser, app, etc.)
- Example: our `/` endpoint **returns the user info in JSON**

2. **Receiving Data (Request)**
- APIs can also accept JSON from clients
- **Example client request:**
```json
{
 "name": "Jane Doe",
 "email": "jane@example.com"
}
```

**The API will read this JSON and perform actions, like saving the data to a database.** \
We’ll cover this in detail next.

practiceProblems.title: Spring Boot API Demonstration - Receiving JSON
practiceProblems.description:
**APIs are not just for sending data**; they can also **receive data from clients**.

In this lab, your **API can accept JSON data**, which is a structured way to send information over the internet. 
**Example client request** (JSON):
```json
{
 "name": "Jane Doe",
 "email": "jane@example.com"
}
```
Give your name and email in JSON format, **Click on `Send JSON`**, You'll get **Response**. 

The client (like a web page, Postman, or another application) sends this data to your API. \
The API reads the JSON automatically and converts it into a Java object behind the scenes.

---

Don’t worry about the Java code here. \
**The key is to understand the data flow**:
```sss
Client → JSON → Spring Boot API → Java Object → Response
```

**Right now, your API is configured to**: 
1. Read the JSON sent by the client.
2. Convert it to a Java object (`UserRequest`).
3. Print it in the console so you can see the data arrived successfully.
4. Return a confirmation message to the client (Response).

Later in the course, **this object can be used to save data to a database or perform other actions**.

pages.title: Understanding the GreetingController Code
pages.content:
Let’s now understand the controller code you used in the previous lab and see **how it handles incoming requests**.

**GreetingController.java**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/greet")
public class GreetingController {
```
**What This Class Does**
- `GreetingController` is a **controller class**
- It is **responsible for handling HTTP requests**
- All API logic for greeting messages is written inside this class
- This is where Spring Boot looks when a request comes in.


**`@RestController`** \
Tells Spring Boot this class **handles API requests** and **sends responses** directly (usually in JSON format), instead of rendering a web page..

**`@RequestMapping("/api/greet")`** \
Tells Spring Boot to send all requests starting with `/api/greet` to this class.

---

**Handling a Simple GET Request** \
Code :
```java
@GetMapping("/hello")
public String helloWorld() {
 return "Hello, World!";
}
```

**`@GetMapping("/hello")`** \
Runs this method when `/api/greet/hello` is called.

---

In this lab, you learned **how to create a GET API using Spring Boot**. \
You used `@GetMapping` to map URLs to methods, returned responses from the API, and tested the endpoints. 

In the next section, you will practice creating GET APIs on your own.

practiceProblems.title: Building Your First GET API
practiceProblems.description:
Imagine you are building an app that manages users. Your app needs to send user information to other parts of the app or even other applications. 

In this demo, we created a `UserController` with several endpoints to:
- Get individual users (Alice, Bob, Charlie)
- Get a list of all users

This is exactly how real-world APIs work—you request data from a URL, and the server sends it back as JSON. 

---

**Before we begin** :
1. Run the application.
2. The API Tester will open automatically.
3. **Enter below URL** one by one -> Click on **"Call API"** and **Observe the Resopnse**

```java
/api/users/alice
/api/users/bob
/api/users/charlie
/api/users/all
```

**Let’s break down how this code works step by step**.

---

**How the Code Works**

**1. Class-level annotations**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
```

- `@RestController` → Marks the class as a controller for APIs.
- `@RequestMapping("/api/users")` → Sets a base URL for all APIs in this controller. \
Every method in this class will start with `/api/users`.

---

**2. Single user endpoints**
```java
@GetMapping("/alice")
@GetMapping("/bob")
@GetMapping("/charlie")
```

`@GetMapping` maps a specific URL → method.

**Examples:**
- `/api/users/alice` → calls `getAlice()` → returns Alice’s info
- `/api/users/bob` → calls `getBob()` → returns Bob’s info
- `/api/users/charlie` → calls `getCharlie()` → returns Charlie’s info

---


**3. List of users endpoint**
```java
@GetMapping("/all")
public List getAllUsers()
```
- Returns a list of User objects.
- Spring Boot automatically converts **Java objects → JSON array**.

Example URL: `/api/users/all` → Returns:

```json
[
 { "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com" },
 { "name": "Bob", "email": "bob@example.com" },
 { "name": "Charlie", "email": "charlie@example.com" }
]
```

practiceProblems.description:
Imagine you are building an app to **manage users**. You want to let clients (frontend apps, Postman, etc.) **add new users** to your system.

In this demo, we created a **UserController** with an endpoint to:
- Add a single user

This is exactly how real-world APIs work — **you send JSON to a URL, the server receives it, stores it, and responds with a confirmation message**.

Note: There is also a **GET endpoint** available to see which users have been added for your better understanding, but **we will not focus on GET here**.

---

**Before we begin** :

1. Run the application.
2. The API Tester will open automatically.
3. Send JSON to the following URLs and observe the response:

**Example Request**

1. POST – Add single user
```sss
POST : /users
```

```json
{
 "name": "David",
 "email": "david@example.com"
}
```

**Response:**
```sss
"User added successfully!"
```

---

**How the Code Works**

- **Single user POST endpoint**
```java
@PostMapping
public String addUser(@RequestBody User user) {
 users.add(user);
 return "User added successfully!";
}
```
- `@PostMapping` → Maps the URL /users to this method.
- `@RequestBody` → Converts incoming JSON into a Java User object automatically.
- `users.add(user)` → Adds the user to the in-memory list.
- `Return message` → Sends a confirmation string back to the client.

---

**Key Points**
- POST APIs → Used to send data to the server.
- `@RequestBody` → Automatically converts JSON → Java objects. \
We'll see `@RequestBody` later in detail.

**For Testing :** \
After sending your `POST` request, you can select **`GET`** and type **`/users` in your API tester*** to see whether your user has been added successfully.

pages.title: Handling Input Data in Spring Boot
pages.content:
Now that you have practiced GET and POST APIs, you know how a client can call an API to fetch or send data. \
But in real applications, APIs don’t work alone — they also need to **accept input data from the client**.

This input data can come in **different ways**, such as:
- Values inside the **URL**
- Values sent as **query parameters**
- Data sent as **JSON in the request body**

---

To handle these different inputs, **Spring Boot provides three important annotations**:

1. **@PathVariable** – \
used when data comes from the **URL path**

2. **@RequestParam** – \
used when data comes from **query parameters**

3. **@RequestBody** – \
used when data comes from the **request body** (JSON)

Let’s see when and why to use each of these annotations — one by one.

pages.title: PathVariable
pages.content:
`@PathVariable` is used when **input data is part of the URL itself**. \
The value is written directly in the URL path and Spring Boot extracts it and passes it to the method.

---

**When do we use it?** \
Use `@PathVariable` when:
- You want to **identify a specific resource**
- The value is **mandatory**
- The URL clearly represents what you are accessing

**Example URL:**
```java
/api/users/101
```
- Here, `101` is a **input value** passed directly in the URL.
- It Extracts values from the URL
- Passes them to the controller method

**Controller Code (Demo)**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

 @GetMapping("/{id}")
 public String getUserById(@PathVariable int id) {
 return "Fetching user with id: " + id;
 }
}
```

**What’s happening here?**

`{id}` → placeholder in the URL \
`@PathVariable int id` → captures the value from the URL \
`Calling /api/users/101` → id becomes $101$

---

**Common use cases:**
- Fetching a user by ID
- Deleting or updating a specific record

pages.title: RequestParam
pages.content:
`@RequestParam` is used when **input data is sent as query parameters in the URL**. \
The value is written after the `?` symbol in the URL and Spring Boot reads it and passes it to the method.

---

**When do we use it?** \
Use `@RequestParam` when:
- The input value is **NOT part of the main URL path**
- The value is often optional
- The data is used for **filtering, searching, or sorting**
- The URL represents an **action**, **NOT** a specific resource

**Example URL:**
```java
/api/users?role=admin
```
- Here, `role` is an **input value passed as a query parameter**
- It Extracts values from query parameters
- Passes them to the controller method



**Controller Code (Demo)**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

 @GetMapping
 public String getUsersByRole(@RequestParam String role) {
 return "Fetching users with role: " + role;
 }
}
```

**What’s happening here?**
- `?role=admin` → query parameter in the URL
- `@RequestParam String role` → captures the value from the URL
- Calling `/api/users?role=admin` → role becomes `admin`

---

**use cases:**
- Searching users by name or role
- Filtering results

pages.title: RequestBody
pages.content:
`@RequestBody` is used when input data is sent **inside the request body** (usually as JSON). \
Spring Boot reads the request body, converts the JSON into a Java object, and passes it to the controller method.

---

**When do we use it?** \
Use `@RequestBody` when:
- You are sending **complex data** (objects, multiple fields)
- Data is coming from a **POST / PUT request**
- Input is **not suitable for the URL**
- You want to send data securely and cleanly

**Example Request Body (JSON):**
```json
{
 "name": "Alice",
 "email": "alice@example.com"
}
```
This data is sent **inside the body**, not in the URL.


**What does it do?**
- Reads data from the HTTP request body
- Converts JSON → Java Object
- Passes the object to the controller method



**Controller Code (Demo)**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

 @PostMapping
 public String addUser(@RequestBody User user) {
 return "User added: " + user.getName();
 }
}
```

**What’s happening here?**
- `@RequestBody User user` → captures JSON from request body
- JSON fields are mapped to the `User` class
- Spring Boot handles conversion automatically

---

**Common use cases:**
- POST & PUT HTTP methods - commonly used with `@RequestBody`
- Creating a new user
- Submitting forms
- Sending login or registration data
- Updating records with multiple fields
